unit.name: The Impact of IT and Cybersecurity
unit.subtitle: Threats to information, protection methods, the law and the wider impact of technology.

lessons.title: Threats to Information
lessons.description: Explore risks to computer-held data and the impact of data loss, theft or manipulation on individuals and businesses.
lessons.content_html:
Risks to Information Held on Computers

Every organisation that uses computers stores information that can be damaged, stolen or misused. Understanding the different types of risk is essential for protecting data and avoiding serious harm to individuals and businesses alike.

Accidental Damage

Not every threat is deliberate. Accidental damage can occur when a user accidentally deletes important files, a hard drive fails without warning, or a power surge corrupts data. Human error is one of the most common causes of data loss in the workplace.

Another accidental risk comes from incorrectly assigned access levels. If a system administrator gives a member of staff access to files they should not see, that employee may unintentionally disclose sensitive information to others or use data in ways that were never intended. This is sometimes called unintended disclosure, and it can have serious legal consequences under data protection law.

Key Fact

Incorrectly assigning access levels is a non-malicious risk that can still result in data breaches, GDPR violations and serious reputational harm for an organisation.

Malicious Software

Malware is an umbrella term for any software deliberately created to cause harm. There are several distinct types that you need to know.

A virus is a program that attaches itself to a legitimate file and spreads when that file is copied or shared. A worm is similar but spreads automatically across networks without needing a host file. A Trojan horse disguises itself as useful software to trick users into installing it, then carries out harmful actions in the background.

Spyware secretly monitors a user's activity, collecting passwords, browsing history or financial details without consent. Ransomware goes further — it locks or encrypts the victim's files and demands a payment, often in cryptocurrency, before restoring access. High-profile ransomware attacks have crippled hospitals, schools and businesses worldwide.

A Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack floods a server or website with so much traffic that it becomes overwhelmed and unavailable to legitimate users. This is often carried out using a network of infected computers called a botnet. Finally, key-logging software silently records every keystroke a user makes, allowing attackers to harvest login credentials and financial data over time.

A virus needs a host file to attach itself to and can only spread when that file is shared by a user. A worm is self-replicating and spreads automatically across a network without any human action required. Both can cause significant damage, but worms tend to spread much faster because they do not rely on user behaviour.

Hacking

Hacking refers to gaining unauthorised access to a computer system or network. However, not all hackers have the same intentions. Security professionals distinguish between three groups using a colour-coded classification.

A white hat hacker works ethically and legally, often employed by organisations to find security vulnerabilities before criminals can exploit them. This is known as penetration testing. A black hat hacker breaks into systems without permission, motivated by financial gain, malice or curiosity, and their actions are illegal. A grey hat hacker sits between the two — they may access systems without permission but typically notify the organisation of vulnerabilities rather than exploiting them maliciously.

A business might hire a white hat hacker to carry out a penetration test — a controlled, legal attempt to break into their own systems. This reveals weaknesses in security before a malicious attacker can find and exploit them. It is a proactive approach that can save an organisation from far more damaging breaches in the future.

Social Engineering

Social engineering exploits human psychology rather than technical flaws. The most common form is phishing — sending emails that appear to come from trusted sources, such as a bank or a manager, to trick recipients into clicking malicious links or entering login credentials. Other techniques include pretexting (inventing a believable scenario to extract information), baiting (leaving infected USB drives where victims will find them) and vishing (voice phishing over the phone).

The Impact of Data Loss, Theft or Manipulation

When data is lost, stolen or altered without authorisation, the consequences can be severe and wide-ranging. Both individuals and businesses face a range of financial, legal, moral and operational impacts.

Financial Implications

Businesses may face enormous costs following a data breach. These include paying ransom demands, funding IT forensics investigations, compensating affected customers and investing in new security infrastructure. A competitor who gains access to confidential pricing strategies or product plans gains an unfair financial advantage that can permanently damage the victim organisation's market position.

Key Fact

Under the UK General Data Protection Regulation (UK GDPR) and the Data Protection Act 2018, organisations can face fines of up to £17.5 million or 4% of global annual turnover for serious data breaches — whichever is higher.

Moral and Legal Implications

Organisations have a moral responsibility to protect personal data entrusted to them by employees, customers and partners. Breaching this trust is not only ethically wrong but also illegal. Failing to comply with UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 can result in regulatory fines, prosecution and mandatory reporting obligations. Individuals whose data is leaked may become victims of identity theft, fraud or blackmail — harm that the organisation is morally accountable for enabling.

Data Manipulation and Loss of Service

Data manipulation occurs when an attacker alters records rather than simply stealing or deleting them. This can be especially damaging because the changes may go undetected for some time. For example, if a hospital's patient records are silently altered, treatment decisions could be based on incorrect information with life-threatening consequences. Loss of service — as seen in DDoS attacks — prevents customers from accessing websites or online platforms, leading to lost sales and eroded trust.

Loss of Intellectual Property and Reputation

Intellectual property (IP) such as product designs, source code, research data or creative content represents a business's competitive advantage. If this is stolen, competitors can replicate innovations without the investment, destroying the original creator's market edge. Alongside this, a business that suffers a publicised data breach often experiences lasting reputational damage. Customers lose confidence, partners withdraw and the business may struggle to recover even after the technical issue is resolved.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
Exam questions often ask you to identify a threat and explain its impact. Always try to link your answer to a specific consequence — for example, a ransomware attack causes loss of service AND financial implications (ransom payment) AND potential loss of reputation. Multi-point answers that show how consequences connect will score higher marks.

When discussing legal implications, refer specifically to UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018 by name — vague references to 'the law' or 'data protection rules' will not score as well in extended-response questions.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Risks to data include accidental damage, incorrectly assigned access levels, malware (viruses, worms, Trojans, spyware, ransomware, DDoS, key-logging), hacking and social engineering.
  • Hackers are classified as white hat (ethical), black hat (criminal) or grey hat (ambiguous intent); only white hat hacking is lawful.
  • Data loss, theft or manipulation can lead to financial loss, legal penalties under UK GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, competitor advantage, data manipulation, loss of service, loss of intellectual property and lasting reputational damage.

practice_questions.text:
Which type of malware encrypts a victim's files and demands payment for the decryption key?
A) Spyware
B) Ransomware
C) Worm
D) Key-logger
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for B) Ransomware.

practice_questions.text: State two types of malware that could be used to attack a business's computer system.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two from: virus / worm / Trojan horse / spyware / ransomware / key-logging software. Maximum 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by social engineering and why it poses a risk to an organisation's data.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a correct definition of social engineering (manipulating people rather than systems). 1 mark for an example such as phishing. 1 mark for explaining the risk, e.g. employees may unknowingly hand over credentials or install malware.

practice_questions.text: Describe, with an example, how a DDoS attack could affect an online retail business.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining what a DDoS attack is (flooding a server with traffic). 1 mark for explaining the immediate effect (server overwhelmed, website goes down). 1 mark for a specific business impact (customers cannot place orders / loss of sales). 1 mark for a further consequence such as loss of customer trust or reputational damage.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the financial and legal implications of a data breach for a medium-sized business that holds customer personal data.
practice_questions.marks: For financial implications: direct costs such as ransom payment, forensic investigation, customer compensation, IT security upgrades (up to 3 marks). For legal implications: fines under UK GDPR / Data Protection Act 2018, mandatory reporting obligations, possible prosecution (up to 3 marks). Credit linkage between the two, e.g. legal fines compound financial loss. Full marks require both dimensions to be discussed with developed reasoning.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the threats posed by hacking and malware to a school that stores student records digitally. Consider the impact on the school, students and any legal obligations. In your answer, weigh up which threat is likely to cause the greatest harm.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8 marks): Balanced evaluation comparing hacking and malware, justifies which poses greater harm with reasoned argument, demonstrates understanding of both technical and human factors, references UK GDPR / DPA 2018, sustained quality of written communication throughout. Secure (5–6 marks): Clear explanation of multiple threats, impacts on school and students (financial, reputational, loss of service, data manipulation), reference to relevant legislation. Developing (3–4 marks): Some explanation of hacking and/or malware impacts with reference to the school context. Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic identification of threats with limited explanation.

lessons.title: Protecting Information
lessons.description: Logical, physical and policy-based methods used to keep data and systems safe from threats.
lessons.content_html:
Why Protecting Information Matters

Every organisation stores sensitive information — customer records, financial data, staff details and confidential business plans. If that information is lost, stolen or tampered with, the consequences can be severe: financial penalties, damaged reputation and loss of customer trust. Protecting information is therefore one of the most important responsibilities of any ICT professional. There are three broad categories of protection: logical, physical and security policies. Each layer addresses a different type of threat, and the strongest protection combines all three.

Logical Protection

Logical protection refers to software and system-based controls that prevent unauthorised access to data. Unlike physical locks, logical controls work by verifying identity and enforcing rules within the digital environment itself. The most common logical measures are access levels, authentication, firewalls, anti-malware applications, password protection and encryption.

Access levels ensure that users can only see and edit the information they need for their role. A sales assistant, for example, might be able to view customer orders but not alter payroll records. This limits the damage a compromised account can do. Authentication is the process of confirming that someone is who they claim to be. It can be single-factor (a password alone) or multi-factor, where a second check — such as a one-time code sent to a mobile phone — is also required. Multi-factor authentication is far harder for an attacker to bypass because stealing a password is not enough on its own.

Firewalls act as gatekeepers between a trusted internal network and untrusted external networks such as the internet. They examine data packets arriving at or leaving the network and block any traffic that does not match the permitted rules. A firewall can be hardware-based (a dedicated device), software-based (installed on individual computers) or a combination of both. Anti-malware applications scan the system for harmful software — viruses, spyware, ransomware — and either quarantine or delete threats before they can cause damage. They also monitor activity in real time, flagging suspicious processes immediately.

Password protection is one of the simplest but most widely used logical controls. Strong passwords — long, combining letters, numbers and symbols — are significantly harder to crack by brute-force attacks. Organisations often enforce a password policy that sets minimum complexity requirements and forces regular changes. Encryption goes further: even if an attacker gains access to data, they cannot read it without the decryption key. Data can be encrypted at rest (stored on a server or device) and in transit (as it travels across a network). HTTPS — visible in your browser address bar — uses encryption to protect web traffic.

Key Fact

The six logical protection methods are: access levels (limit what users can do), authentication (verify identity), firewalls (filter network traffic), anti-malware applications (detect and remove threats), password protection (control login access) and encryption (scramble data so it cannot be read without a key).

Authentication answers the question "who are you?" — it verifies identity before granting any access at all. Access levels answer the question "what are you allowed to do?" — they define what an already-authenticated user is permitted to see or change. Both work together: authentication is the door, and access levels are the rooms within the building that each person is allowed to enter. A school network, for example, might authenticate every pupil with a username and password, but access levels ensure that pupils cannot edit teacher mark books or administrative records.

Physical Protection

Even the strongest logical controls cannot help if an unauthorised person can walk up to a server and physically remove the hard drive. Physical protection addresses this by controlling and monitoring access to the real-world spaces and hardware where data is stored. Physical measures include locks, biometrics, the location of hardware, backup systems and security staff.

Locks are the most straightforward physical control — server rooms, filing cabinets and computer cases can all be locked to prevent unauthorised access. Biometrics offer a higher level of physical access control by using unique bodily characteristics: fingerprint scanners, iris recognition and facial recognition are all examples. Unlike keys or access cards, biometric data cannot easily be passed to another person or forgotten. The location of hardware also matters: servers and network equipment should be housed in dedicated secure rooms rather than shared offices, and ideally not on ground floor or basement levels where flooding or break-in risk is higher.

Backup systems protect against the permanent loss of data due to hardware failure, fire, flood or malicious deletion. A good backup strategy follows the 3-2-1 rule: keep three copies of data, on two different types of storage, with one copy held off-site. Off-site backups ensure that a single disaster — a fire destroying an office, for example — cannot wipe all copies simultaneously. Security staff provide a human layer of protection: patrolling premises, monitoring CCTV, checking visitor identity and responding to incidents in real time. Human oversight catches threats that automated systems might miss, such as an employee behaving suspiciously or a tailgating attempt at a secure door.

Key Fact

The five physical protection methods are: locks (restrict physical access), biometrics (verify identity using body characteristics), location of hardware (keep servers in secure, appropriate environments), backup systems (maintain copies of data in multiple locations) and security staff (human monitoring and response). Physical and logical measures work best in combination.

Backup systems are classified as physical protection because the key decisions involved — where to store the backup media, how many copies to hold, whether to keep one off-site — all concern physical hardware and location. Even cloud backups rely on physical servers in a different location. The protection they provide is resilience against physical threats (fire, flood, hardware failure) rather than against logical threats like malware, though they do incidentally protect against ransomware too. In an exam, listing backup systems under physical protection is correct; listing it under logical would typically lose the mark.

Security Policies

Technology alone cannot protect an organisation if people do not use it correctly. Security policies are documented rules and procedures that govern how staff handle information and respond to incidents. The three main policies covered in this topic are: disaster recovery, staff responsibilities and the acceptable use policy.

A disaster recovery plan is a documented procedure that sets out exactly what an organisation will do if a major incident — a cyberattack, a fire or a flood — disrupts normal operations. It identifies which systems must be restored first, who is responsible for each action, where backup data is held and how long restoration should take. Without a disaster recovery plan, organisations often make chaotic decisions under pressure, taking far longer to recover than necessary. Staff responsibilities policies make clear what each employee is expected to do to protect information — for example, not sharing passwords, locking their computer screen when leaving their desk and reporting any suspicious emails or activity immediately.

An acceptable use policy (AUP) is a written agreement that tells users what they are and are not allowed to do with an organisation's ICT systems. It typically covers rules on personal use, prohibited websites, the installation of unauthorised software and the handling of sensitive data. Employees usually sign an AUP when they join an organisation. Staff training is essential because many security breaches are caused by human error rather than sophisticated technical attacks — clicking on a phishing link, using a weak password or accidentally emailing a file to the wrong person. Regular training keeps staff aware of current threats and reminds them of their responsibilities.
lessons.exam_tip_html:
In questions that ask you to identify a method of protection, always be precise about which category it belongs to. A firewall is a logical measure; a biometric scanner is a physical measure; a disaster recovery plan is a security policy. Mixing up the categories is a common mistake that loses marks. For extended-answer questions, the strongest responses explain how two or three measures work together — for example, explaining how encryption (logical) protects data even if a backup drive (physical) is stolen.

When evaluating which measures are most important, be careful not to dismiss any category completely. Full marks require a balanced argument: logical controls are useless if a thief walks out with the server; physical controls are useless if a remote hacker can access the system over the internet; and both are undermined by staff who ignore the acceptable use policy. The best protection is always layered.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Logical protection uses software-based controls — access levels, authentication, firewalls, anti-malware, password protection and encryption — to prevent unauthorised digital access to data.
  • Physical protection uses tangible measures — locks, biometrics, hardware location, backup systems and security staff — to prevent unauthorised physical access to equipment and data.
  • Security policies — disaster recovery plans, staff responsibility guidelines, acceptable use policies and staff training — ensure that people use technology correctly and respond effectively when something goes wrong.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of logical protection?
A) Keeping a server in a locked room
B) Employing security guards to patrol the building
C) Using encryption to scramble stored data
D) Storing backup drives off-site
practice_questions.marks: C) Using encryption to scramble stored data [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two physical protection methods an organisation can use to keep its data safe.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct methods from: locks / biometrics / location of hardware / backup systems / security staff. Answers must clearly identify a physical method; vague answers such as "keeping data safe" score 0. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how a firewall helps to protect an organisation's network from unauthorised access.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. "a firewall blocks unwanted traffic"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "a firewall examines data packets entering and leaving the network, comparing them against a set of rules, and blocks any traffic that does not meet those rules"). A further developed explanation or reference to hardware vs software firewalls scores 3 marks (e.g. add "this prevents hackers from establishing unauthorised connections to internal systems, even if the organisation's own devices have been compromised"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what an acceptable use policy is and give one example of a rule it might contain.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): an acceptable use policy (AUP) is a documented agreement between an organisation and its staff that sets out what employees are and are not permitted to do when using the organisation's ICT systems (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement that it is a set of rules for computer use).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, the AUP might state that staff must not install personal software on work computers, because unauthorised software could contain malware that compromises the whole network (2 marks for a specific, applied example with a reason; 1 mark for a vague example without explanation). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A small business stores customer payment details on a local server. Last month it suffered a ransomware attack that encrypted all its files and demanded a ransom. The business had no backup copies of its data and no disaster recovery plan.

Discuss the protection measures the business should put in place to prevent a similar incident and to recover more effectively in future.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two categories of protection with developed explanation and clear reference to the scenario. For example: anti-malware software would detect and block ransomware before it executes; encryption of the data at rest means that even if ransomware gains access, the data is already protected; a regular off-site backup strategy ensures that if files are encrypted by ransomware, a clean copy can be restored without paying the ransom; a disaster recovery plan ensures staff know exactly what steps to take, minimising downtime. Discussion notes that multiple layers are needed because no single measure is sufficient.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two measures identified and explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two measures identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A large hospital stores patient medical records digitally. It employs a team of IT security staff, uses biometric scanners on all server room doors, requires multi-factor authentication for all staff logins and enforces a strict acceptable use policy.

Evaluate the extent to which the hospital's current security measures are sufficient to protect patient data from all types of threat.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation acknowledging the strengths of the existing measures — biometrics prevent unauthorised physical entry to server rooms; multi-factor authentication makes remote account compromise very difficult; the AUP reduces risk of human error; security staff provide active monitoring. Counter-argument identifies gaps: no mention of encryption (data in transit or at rest could be intercepted), no mention of firewalls (network perimeter unprotected), no mention of a disaster recovery plan (if an incident does occur, recovery may be chaotic), and no mention of staff training (AUP alone does not guarantee staff understand current threats like phishing). Substantiated judgement — e.g. the hospital has strong physical and authentication controls but logical and policy gaps remain, particularly encryption and a formal recovery procedure, meaning the current measures are not fully sufficient.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two strengths and two weaknesses identified, with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely one-sided with limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development and no evaluation. [8 marks]

glossary_terms.definition: Software-based controls that restrict or regulate access to digital information and systems, such as passwords, firewalls and encryption.
The process of verifying a user's identity before granting access, typically through passwords, security tokens or biometric data.
A security system that monitors and filters network traffic based on defined rules, blocking unauthorised connections.
The process of converting readable data into a scrambled format that can only be decoded by someone with the correct key.
Security technology that uses unique biological characteristics such as fingerprints, iris patterns or facial recognition to verify identity.

lessons.title: Moral, Ethical and Legal Issues
lessons.description: How moral, ethical and legal frameworks govern the use of IT and protect individuals online.
lessons.content_html:
Why Ethics and Law Matter in IT

Technology has transformed how we live, work and communicate — but it has also created new ways for individuals and organisations to cause harm, whether intentionally or accidentally. Ethics in IT means thinking carefully about the impact our choices have on other people, from sharing someone's photo without asking to building a system that stores private health records. Laws exist to enforce the most serious of these expectations, but our personal sense of right and wrong — our moral compass — matters just as much.

This lesson examines the key moral and ethical issues raised by modern IT, and then looks at the specific laws that protect computer users in the United Kingdom. Knowing these laws by name and date is essential — examiners expect you to name them correctly.

Moral and Ethical Issues

Privacy and Security

Privacy is one of the most contested issues in the digital age. Every time you use a website, app or search engine, data about you can be collected, stored and analysed. Some of this is harmless — a streaming service remembering your viewing history — but the same technology can be used to build detailed profiles of individuals without their knowledge or meaningful consent. The moral question is whether organisations have the right to gather and profit from this data, even when users technically agreed to lengthy terms and conditions that most people never read.

Security goes hand in hand with privacy. When companies collect large volumes of personal data, they take on a responsibility to protect it. Poor security practices — weak passwords, unencrypted databases, unpatched software — can lead to breaches that expose millions of people to identity theft, fraud and harassment.

Key Fact

Cookies are small text files stored on your device by websites. Multinational companies use them to track browsing behaviour across many sites, building detailed profiles of your interests, habits and purchasing patterns — often without users fully realising it.

Cookies and Data Collection by Multinational Companies

Large technology companies such as search engines and social media platforms generate enormous revenue by selling advertising based on user data. Cookies allow these companies to follow users across the web, recording which pages they visit, how long they stay and what they purchase. The ethical concern is that this tracking is often opaque — users consent to a broad privacy policy without understanding that their data may be sold to third parties, used to influence their political views or shared with government agencies.

The scale of data collection by multinational companies is staggering. A single large platform may hold data on billions of individuals. This creates a power imbalance: ordinary users have little control over how their information is used, while corporations and advertisers benefit commercially.

Monitoring of Individuals

Individuals can be monitored in many ways — employers checking staff emails, governments intercepting private communications, or apps tracking a phone's GPS location. Some monitoring is legitimate: parents using parental controls to protect young children, or employers monitoring company devices to prevent data leaks. However, covert or excessive monitoring raises serious ethical questions about trust, autonomy and human rights. The line between reasonable oversight and invasive surveillance is often unclear, and different people will draw it in different places.

Something can be legal yet still ethically questionable. An employer might have the legal right to read staff emails on company devices, but if employees are not told this is happening, many would consider it a breach of trust. Ethics is about what we ought to do, not just what we are allowed to do. Monitoring without transparency undermines personal dignity and can damage relationships between institutions and the individuals they serve.

Impact of Data Loss or Damage

When data is lost, corrupted or stolen, the consequences can be severe. At a personal level, someone whose bank details are exposed in a breach may face fraud, financial loss and months of stress resolving the problem. At an organisational level, a hospital losing patient records could delay treatment and put lives at risk. For businesses, a major breach can destroy customer trust overnight and result in large regulatory fines. Morally, this means everyone involved in storing or handling data — from software developers to system administrators — carries a responsibility to treat that data with care.

Key Fact

Data loss or damage can affect individuals through identity theft and financial harm, and organisations through regulatory fines, reputational damage and loss of customer trust. Under GDPR, serious breaches must be reported to the Information Commissioner's Office within 72 hours.

Laws That Protect Computer Users

The United Kingdom has a range of laws designed to protect individuals and ensure technology is used responsibly. You need to know the full name and year of each one.

General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) 2018

The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which came into force in 2018, is the main law governing how personal data must be handled. It gives individuals the right to access data held about them, correct inaccurate data and request deletion (the "right to be forgotten"). Organisations must have a clear lawful basis for processing personal data — for example, consent, a contractual obligation or a legitimate interest. GDPR applies to any organisation that processes the data of UK or EU citizens, regardless of where the organisation is based.

Data Protection Act (DPA) 1998

Before GDPR, the Data Protection Act 1998 was the primary data-protection law in the UK. It set out eight principles governing the use of personal data, including that data must be processed fairly and lawfully, held for specified purposes only, kept accurate and up to date, not retained longer than necessary, and kept secure. When GDPR was adopted in 2018, the Data Protection Act was updated (the Data Protection Act 2018 incorporated GDPR into UK law), but examination questions sometimes refer to the original 1998 Act, so you should be familiar with both.

Computer Misuse Act 1990

The Computer Misuse Act 1990 criminalises three main offences: unauthorised access to computer material (for example, guessing someone's password to read their emails), unauthorised access with intent to commit further offences (such as breaking into a company's server to steal financial data), and unauthorised modification of computer material (including installing malware or deleting files). This law is the primary weapon against hacking, ransomware attacks and other forms of cybercrime in the UK.

The three offences are: (1) unauthorised access to computer material — simply logging into a system without permission; (2) unauthorised access with intent to commit or facilitate further offences — breaking in with the aim of committing fraud or theft; (3) unauthorised modification of computer material — deliberately altering, deleting or corrupting data or programs, which includes deploying viruses or ransomware.

Communications Act 2003

The Communications Act 2003 covers the misuse of electronic communications networks. It makes it an offence to send grossly offensive, indecent, obscene or menacing messages using a public electronic communications network, which includes social media, messaging apps and email. This law is frequently used in cases involving cyberbullying, threatening messages and online harassment.

Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA)

The Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 governs how government agencies and law enforcement may lawfully intercept and monitor communications. It sets out strict rules about when surveillance, covert investigation and the interception of private messages are permitted, requiring appropriate authorisation. While it enables legitimate national security activity, it also acts as a safeguard against state overreach — agencies must follow defined processes rather than conducting unlimited surveillance.

Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988

The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects intellectual property, including software, music, images and written content. It is illegal to copy, distribute or reproduce protected material without permission from the rights holder. In an IT context, this means that downloading pirated software, sharing copyrighted music files or reproducing images from the internet without a licence can all be criminal offences. Creators are automatically protected as soon as they produce original work — they do not need to register a copyright.

Health and Safety Legislation

Health and safety law applies to the physical use of computer equipment in the workplace. The Health and Safety (Display Screen Equipment) Regulations 1992 require employers to assess and reduce risks from the prolonged use of screens and keyboards. This includes providing adjustable chairs, adequate lighting, regular breaks and eye tests. Failure to follow these regulations can lead to conditions such as repetitive strain injury (RSI), eye strain and musculoskeletal problems. Employers have a legal duty to make workstations safe.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Exam questions often ask you to "name" or "state" a law — always include the full name and the correct year. For example, write "Computer Misuse Act 1990" rather than just "the hacking law". A common mistake is confusing the Data Protection Act 1998 with GDPR 2018 — remember that GDPR replaced the DPA as the main data-protection law in 2018, but the 1998 Act is still worth knowing as the predecessor. When evaluating moral and ethical issues, make sure you discuss both sides: who benefits from monitoring or data collection, and who is harmed by it.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Moral and ethical issues in IT include privacy, cookie-based surveillance, monitoring of individuals, and the serious consequences of data loss or damage.
  • The key laws protecting computer users are: GDPR 2018, Data Protection Act 1998, Computer Misuse Act 1990, Communications Act 2003, Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000, Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, and Health and Safety legislation.
  • Always use the full name and correct year of a law in exam answers, and be ready to explain what each law covers with a real-world example.

lessons.title: Society, Environment and Digital Footprint
lessons.description: How ICT reshapes work, society and the environment — and how your digital footprint affects your online identity.
lessons.content_html:
How ICT Has Changed the Way We Work

Advances in digital technology have transformed employment in two main ways: some jobs have disappeared while entirely new ones have been created. Changing employment patterns mean that roles in manufacturing, retail checkout, and telephone directories have shrunk dramatically as automation and digital systems have taken over. At the same time, demand for software developers, data analysts, cybersecurity specialists and social media managers has surged. Workers left behind by these shifts often need to undergo retraining to remain employable — government and employer-funded programmes help workers move into growing sectors like tech support, digital marketing and cloud computing.

ICT has also changed where and how people collaborate. Hot-desking is an arrangement where no employee has a fixed desk — workers book a space when they need one, reducing office costs and encouraging cross-team interaction. Teleworking (or homeworking) lets staff perform their duties from home, cutting commuting time and giving greater flexibility. This has been made possible by broadband internet, cloud storage and collaboration tools such as shared documents and instant messaging. Videoconferencing tools — including Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meet — allow real-time face-to-face meetings between people in different cities or countries, reducing the need for expensive and time-consuming business travel.

Key Fact

Teleworking and videoconferencing reduce the need for daily commuting and long-haul business travel. Fewer car journeys and flights directly lower carbon dioxide emissions and ease congestion on road networks — a genuine environmental benefit of ICT adoption.

Effects on Transport and Traditional Media

The spread of ICT has reduced physical travel in multiple ways. Online shopping means consumers no longer need to visit a high street, lowering personal car use — though it has simultaneously increased delivery van traffic. Videoconferencing and virtual events have slashed the number of business flights taken each year. However, the growth of data centres and the manufacture of digital devices consume significant amounts of energy, partly offsetting these transport savings.

Traditional media — newspapers, magazines, free-to-air television and physical music stores — has been disrupted profoundly. Readers now consume news through websites, apps and social media feeds rather than buying a printed newspaper. Streaming services have replaced CD and DVD purchases. Many regional newspapers have closed because advertising revenue shifted to online platforms. While this makes information faster and cheaper to access, it has also reduced employment in printing, distribution and traditional journalism.

Drones, Green IT and E-Waste

Drones are unmanned aerial vehicles controlled digitally. They are used for parcel delivery, agricultural monitoring, search-and-rescue operations, film-making and infrastructure inspection. Commercially, drones can reach remote areas faster and more cheaply than road vehicles; however, they raise concerns about privacy, noise pollution, airspace regulation and collision risk with manned aircraft.

Green IT refers to practices and technologies designed to reduce the environmental impact of computing — for example, energy-efficient server hardware, renewable-powered data centres, device recycling programmes and power-saving settings on consumer hardware. In contrast, non-green IT involves high energy consumption, short product lifecycles, planned obsolescence and the disposal of working equipment simply to follow trends. The global shift towards cloud computing and AI services has dramatically increased energy demand from data centres, raising questions about whether ICT is truly becoming more sustainable.

Key Fact

E-waste (electronic waste) is one of the fastest-growing waste streams globally. Discarded phones, laptops and monitors often contain hazardous materials including lead, mercury and cadmium. Much e-waste from wealthy countries is illegally shipped to lower-income nations where it is processed in unsafe conditions, causing serious harm to local communities and ecosystems.

The manufacture of digital devices depends on rare-earth element mining. Elements such as neodymium, cobalt and lithium are essential for batteries, screens and circuit boards, but extracting them causes significant environmental damage — deforestation, water contamination, and soil degradation in mining regions. Mining is often concentrated in a small number of countries, creating geopolitical supply-chain risks and raising ethical concerns about labour conditions.

The Digital Divide, Social Media and Net Neutrality

Access to digital technology is not equal. The digital divide describes this inequality. Locally, elderly people, those on low incomes and people in rural areas may lack devices or fast broadband. Globally, large parts of sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia and rural South America have limited or no internet connectivity. The digital divide reinforces existing inequalities — those without access are excluded from online education, e-commerce, telehealth and remote work opportunities. Solutions include government broadband investment, subsidised devices and community digital skills programmes.

Global production lines mean that the components inside a single smartphone may be designed in the USA, manufactured in Taiwan, assembled in China, and sold across Europe — a supply chain that depends entirely on ICT to coordinate, track and manage orders in real time. While this lowers costs and enables mass production, it also creates ethical issues around labour standards and increases carbon emissions from global freight.

Social media platforms have connected billions of people, enabling community building, political participation and rapid information sharing. However, they have also enabled cyberbullying — the deliberate use of digital platforms to harass, threaten or humiliate others — and the rapid spread of fake news, which is fabricated or deliberately misleading content designed to look like credible reporting. Both problems have been linked to increased anxiety, depression and social polarisation, particularly among young people.

Net neutrality is the principle that internet service providers should treat all online data equally — they should not slow down, block or charge more for access to specific websites or services. Supporters argue net neutrality is essential for a free and open internet; opponents argue that providers should be able to manage network traffic and charge heavy users more. Digital addiction — compulsive use of social media, gaming or streaming — is a growing mental health concern, with excessive screen time linked to sleep disruption, reduced concentration and lower self-esteem.

A passive digital footprint is data collected about you without your direct knowledge or active input — for example, websites logging your IP address, cookies tracking your browsing history, or a retailer storing your purchase patterns. An active digital footprint is created deliberately when you choose to share information online — posting on social media, writing a blog comment, completing an online form or uploading a photo. Most people have both types simultaneously, but many are unaware of the extent of their passive footprint, which can be bought and sold by data brokers without explicit consent.

Digital Footprint, Online Identity and Identity Theft

Every time you use the internet, you leave a trail of data behind you — this is your digital footprint. Posts on social media, likes, comments, photographs, search queries, online purchases, app usage and location data all contribute to a detailed picture of who you are, what you believe, how you spend your time and money, and who you know. This digital profile can be accessed by employers screening job candidates, universities verifying applicants, advertisers targeting content, and — in some cases — malicious individuals seeking to exploit it.

Your online identity is the impression of yourself you create through digital activity. A carefully managed online identity — a professional LinkedIn profile, a thoughtful social media presence, a portfolio website — can open doors to employment and networking. An unmanaged or negative online identity — offensive posts, complaints from former employers visible in public comments, photographs from social situations — can close those same doors. Once published, online content is extremely difficult to fully remove, and even deleted posts may have been screenshotted and reshared.

Identity theft occurs when a criminal obtains enough personal information about someone — name, address, date of birth, financial details or account credentials — to impersonate them, typically for financial fraud. Data harvested from social media posts, phishing emails, data breaches and weak passwords are all common pathways to identity theft. The consequences include damaged credit ratings, fraudulent loans or purchases in the victim's name, and significant distress and time spent recovering the situation.

Sharing inappropriate images online carries serious long-term risks. Once an image has been sent or posted, the sender loses control over it — it can be saved, forwarded and republished indefinitely. Images that seem harmless in a social context (for example, a photograph at a party) may damage future employment prospects or university applications if seen out of context. More seriously, the sharing of intimate or explicit images without consent is a criminal offence under current UK law. Young people can be targeted by people who use social media to build false trust before requesting or distributing images — a process known as grooming. The permanence of digital content means that the impact of sharing a harmful image can last for years after the original event.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Exam questions on this topic often ask you to "explain" or "discuss" rather than simply list. When a question asks you to explain the impact of the digital divide, go beyond saying access is unequal — describe the concrete consequences (excluded from online education, unable to access remote work, disadvantaged in job applications) and show you understand both the local and global dimension. For questions about digital footprints, always distinguish passive from active, and link your answer to a specific risk such as identity theft or reputational damage. Six- and eight-mark questions on social media issues reward balanced answers that acknowledge benefits as well as harms.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • ICT has transformed employment through automation and remote working, but creates environmental costs through e-waste, rare-earth mining and energy-hungry data centres — green IT practices aim to reduce this impact.
  • Social media enables connection and information sharing but also drives cyberbullying, fake news, digital addiction and mental health problems; net neutrality determines whether all users access the internet on equal terms.
  • Your digital footprint — both the data you actively share and the data passively collected about you — shapes your online identity and can expose you to identity theft, reputational harm and the lasting consequences of sharing inappropriate images.

practice_questions.text: State two environmental problems caused by the disposal of digital devices (e-waste).
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: release of toxic/hazardous materials (lead, mercury, cadmium) into soil or water / illegal export to lower-income countries where it is unsafely processed / contamination of local ecosystems / harm to communities in processing areas. Answers that repeat the same idea score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how teleworking can have both a positive and a negative effect on transport.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "teleworking reduces the number of commuters on the road"). Development of a positive effect scores 2 marks (e.g. "fewer daily commuter journeys means less road congestion and lower vehicle emissions, reducing the carbon footprint of those workers"). A negative counter-point scores 3 marks (e.g. "however, the growth of online shopping linked to home-based lifestyles has increased delivery vehicle journeys, which partially offsets the commuting reduction"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the digital divide and give one example of how it affects people at a local level.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the digital divide is the gap between those who have reliable, affordable access to digital technology and the internet and those who do not; it can exist within a country (local) as well as between countries (global) (2 marks for a clear developed description covering both access and consequence; 1 mark for a basic definition without development).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, an elderly person in a rural area with no broadband connection cannot access online job boards, telehealth services or online banking, placing them at a significant disadvantage compared with well-connected urban residents (2 marks for a specific, applied example with the disadvantage identified; 1 mark for a vague example without identifying the impact). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impact of social media on individuals and society, including both benefits and drawbacks.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two benefits (e.g. global connection and community building; rapid sharing of important information; political participation; support networks for isolated individuals) and at least two drawbacks (e.g. cyberbullying linked to mental health problems; spread of fake news and misinformation; digital addiction and reduced attention span; privacy risks from oversharing personal data) with clear development and some reference to impact on real people or society.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least two points on each side, briefly explained.
Developing (2 marks): Points largely one-sided or undeveloped.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A young person regularly posts personal updates, holiday photographs and location tags on a public social media profile. They have also signed up to several apps using the same email address and a simple password.

Evaluate the extent to which managing your digital footprint effectively can reduce the risk of identity theft and reputational harm.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying multiple active and passive footprint risks in the scenario (public posts reveal personal details; location tags enable tracking; reused simple passwords increase credential theft risk; passive data collected by apps). Explores how active management reduces risk (privacy settings limit public visibility; strong unique passwords and two-factor authentication reduce account compromise; careful review of what is posted protects reputation). Counter-argument acknowledges limits (passive data collection continues regardless of user choices; data brokers compile profiles from many sources; once data is shared it may be impossible to fully remove). A substantiated judgement — e.g. effective digital footprint management significantly reduces active risks but cannot eliminate passive data harvesting, so individuals should combine careful posting habits with regular privacy setting reviews and strong account security.
Secure (5-6 marks): At least two points on each side of the argument, some applied to the scenario, with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points largely one-sided.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with little development and no evaluative judgement. [8 marks]
